issues.issue: The execution date is left incomplete — "on the Ist day of ____ 1999" has no month, so the date of making cannot be determined from the instrument itself. That blank is a mechanical defect going to when the parties' obligations attached.
The recited making date of 1999 cannot be squared with Section 11 (Effective Date), which states the Agreement is effective in 1997, leaving two inconsistent commencement dates in the same document.

The lettered sub-paragraphs (a., b., c., &) are detached from the duties they are supposed to introduce, and the number of listed duties does not match the number of letters, so the enumeration cannot be applied as written. "Be responsible for the collection of all investment income" also states a duty of result without any stated standard of care.

Paragraph (b) lets the Custodian delegate "such ministerial and other non-discretionary duties as it sees fit" and "rely upon such information furnished by such agents"; the boundary between ministerial/non-discretionary and discretionary duties, and the reach of the reliance protection, are undefined. Paragraph (a) also reads "Hold assets in the nominee selected by the Custodian", apparently omitting "name".

"Such other reports as the Owners may reasonably request, including reports to the Owner's accountants or other examiners as may be necessary" fixes no boundary: "reasonably request", "other examiners" and "as may be necessary" are all open-ended. The catch-all sits against no meaningful specification of what reports are owed.

Compensation is fixed only by reference to "Schedule A attached to this Agreement as amended from time to time by the parties", and it is unclear whether "as amended" qualifies the Schedule or the Agreement. The pricing term is therefore wholly extrinsic.

No Schedule A appears anywhere in the executed instrument, so the fee term cross-refers to a document the contract as a whole does not contain, unlike Section 8 which sets out its particulars in full.

"Out-of-pocket expenses during the reasonable performance of the Custodian's duties" misplaces the reasonableness qualifier — it modifies "performance" rather than the expenses, so it is unclear whether unreasonable expenses are reimbursable. "Out-of-pocket" is itself undefined against the fee schedule.

"Entitled to rely on the oral advice as confirmed in writing or written advice of such persons" is syntactically ambiguous: it can mean oral advice is protected only once confirmed in writing, or that oral advice may be acted on with confirmation to follow. That distinction decides who bears the loss on an unconfirmed oral instruction.

"Any fees remaining outstanding and balances owing to the Custodian" is undefined — "balances owing" could reach beyond fees and expenses to any claim the Custodian asserts, and "may be withheld" gives an unmeasured self-help right.

A unilateral right to withhold assets is difficult to square with Section 15, under which custodied securities "shall be withdrawable upon the demand of the Owner", and with Section 6's delivery obligation on termination.

"Any and all claims, liabilities, and expenses ... which Custodian may incur by reason of its acting as Custodian" does not say whether it covers only third-party claims or also first-party claims by the Owner against the Custodian. That is the classic construction fight in a broad indemnity.

Read as a first-party indemnity it would neutralise Section 21, under which the Custodian indemnifies the Owner for losses caused by its own officers' negligence or dishonesty, so the two indemnities pull in opposite directions.

The carve-out turns on whether the "Custodian has committed negligence or malfeasance", neither term defined, and does not say whether the acts of agents employed under Section 2(b) are the Custodian's. It also disapplies "the indemnification provisions of the Agreement" generally rather than only Section 7.

Because it disapplies "the indemnification provisions of the Agreement" without limitation, it can be read to switch off Section 21's indemnity running the other way, which would be perverse since Section 21 is itself triggered by Custodian negligence.

Section 9 makes the Custodian's books and practices "subject to examination by the Owner" without qualification, while Section 17 permits examination only on the Custodian's premises, during business hours, on reasonable notice and "only upon furnishing ... written instructions" from an officer. The two access rights cannot both operate as written.
